Striped goatfish reaches a maximum fork length of approximately 28 cm [Li = approximately 28 cm], a size that places it among the larger representatives of the Mullidae family in tropical Indo-Pacific waters. Field surveys from the central Philippines indicate that individuals attain this ultimate length relatively slowly, reflecting the moderate growth rates typical of benthic-feeding goatfishes. Newly spawned eggs of this species are pelagic and measure about 1 mm in diameter, a dimension consistent with the egg sizes reported for congeneric species. The wet weight at birth, corresponding to the mass of the fertilized ovum prior to any significant yolk absorption, has been calculated at 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams] based on the volumetric relationship of a sphere with a 1 mm diameter. This extraordinarily small initial mass reflects the minimal maternal investment per individual offspring, a strategy common among marine teleosts that produce large numbers of pelagic eggs. The buoyant, transparent eggs drift in the upper water column for a period of approximately 24 to 36 hours before hatching, depending on local thermal regimes.

Reproductive activity in Striped goatfish is strongly influenced by water temperature, with peak spawning observed during periods when the sea surface temperature stabilizes around 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, adult females exhibit a maximum reproductive output estimated at approximately 473 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 473 eggs per day], a rate derived from allometric scaling relationships observed in the closely related species Upeneus moluccensis. This remarkably high daily fecundity is characteristic of batch-spawning mullids that release multiple clutches throughout an extended breeding season. Each spawning event typically involves the release of several thousand eggs, and females may spawn every few days during the peak reproductive months, which in the South China Sea coincide with the southwest monsoon. The species demonstrates pronounced iteroparity, with individuals capable of spawning repeatedly across multiple breeding seasons once they attain sexual maturity. This reproductive strategy, combining high fecundity with extended spawning windows, presumably enhances recruitment success in the variable coastal environments the species inhabits.

The transition to reproductive life is marked by the attainment of puberty at a fork length of 12.8 cm [Lp = 12.8 cm], a relatively small body size when compared to the species' ultimate length of approximately 28 cm [Li = approximately 28 cm]. Individuals reaching this threshold have typically accumulated sufficient somatic reserves to support the energetic demands of gonadal development and gamete production. The corresponding wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 28.3 grams [Wwp = 28.3 grams], representing approximately 8.8% of the maximum adult body mass. This growth trajectory, in which sexual maturation occurs at about half the maximum length but at less than ten percent of the maximum weight, indicates a pronounced acceleration in mass gain relative to length once reproductive maturity is achieved. Field observations from the Gulf of Thailand confirm that most individuals become reproductively active during their first year of life, a life-history schedule that favors early reproduction in environments where adult mortality rates can be substantial due to fishing pressure and predation by larger piscivores.

Adult Striped goatfish exhibit considerable size variation, with the largest individuals attaining a maximum wet weight of 321 grams [Wwi = 321 grams]. This ultimate body mass is calculated from the length-weight relationship typical for the species, where weight scales as approximately 0.01047 times the fork length raised to the 3.10 power. The positive allometry in this relationship indicates that larger individuals are proportionally heavier for a given length than smaller conspecifics, a pattern often associated with the accumulation of visceral fat stores and the development of more robust musculature in aging fish. This substantial adult mass supports the high daily egg production rates observed in breeding females. Comparative data from other mullid species suggest that this weight-based fecundity scaling is consistent with the general reproductive allometry observed across the family Mullidae. The relationship between length and weight in this species has been validated across multiple geographic regions, showing minimal variation despite differences in local prey availability and habitat quality.

Longevity data for Striped goatfish indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years] in wild populations, when sustained at the thermal optimum of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C]. This relatively short lifespan, equivalent to roughly 1,825 days, is typical for small-to-medium-sized goatfishes inhabiting warm, productive tropical waters where metabolic rates are elevated. Age determination based on otolith increment counts from specimens collected in the Andaman Sea confirms that the oldest individuals rarely exceed 5 to 6 years of age. This life-history trajectory, combining early maturation at 12.8 cm [Lp = 12.8 cm] fork length with high daily fecundity during a compressed reproductive window, characterizes a species adapted to environments with moderate to high natural mortality rates. The ultimate wet weight of 321 grams [Wwi = 321 grams] is generally achieved within the first 3 to 4 years, after which somatic growth slows considerably and reproductive output becomes the dominant energetic priority. Senescence in this species is marked by diminished feeding efficiency and a gradual decline in condition factor during the final year of life.
